lead: A satellite hands you a grid of digital numbers, not a map. Digital image processing corrects that grid, stretches and filters it so the eye can read it, and then sorts every pixel into a class such as water, crop or built-up. An error matrix then says how far to trust the labels.
prereq: You need: the spectral signatures, the four resolutions and the keys of visual image interpretation, which become the training classes.

blocks.text: A digital image is a grid of pixels, each holding a digital number (DN) at the sensor's radiometric resolution, 0 to 255 for an 8-bit image. One grid is one band; a multispectral image stacks several bands pixel for pixel, so all bands at row 120, column 45 describe the same patch of ground.

Radiometric correction fixes brightness. Calibration turns DNs into radiance and removes detector drift; sun-angle correction divides by the cosine of the solar zenith angle, so a low winter sun does not make the ground look falsely dark; haze correction subtracts the path radiance that lifts even the darkest pixel above zero.

Geometric correction fixes position. Ground control points (GCPs) are features, such as a road junction, a tank bund or a bridge, whose image and map coordinates are both known. A transformation is fitted through them and the image is resampled onto the map grid. Nearest neighbour copies the closest original DN and keeps values intact. Bilinear interpolation takes the four nearest input pixels and averages them with weights that fall with distance, so the result looks smoother but invents new DN values.

A histogram counts how many pixels carry each DN. A raw scene often fills only a narrow slice of the range because of haze or weak contrast, so it looks grey and flat. A linear contrast stretch pulls the used range out to the full display range.

blocks.where: DN(in) is the input digital number; min and max are the lowest and highest values kept, read from the histogram; DN(out) is the stretched value, clipped to 0–255; 255 is the top of an 8-bit display.

blocks.text: Histogram equalisation is a stronger, non-linear stretch. It reassigns values so every brightness level holds roughly the same number of pixels. Detail in dark forest opens up, but noise in a clear reservoir can be exaggerated.

A spatial filter slides a small kernel, usually 3 × 3, across the image. A low-pass kernel gives every cell the weight 1/9, so the output is the average of the nine cells in the window, centre included: noise is smoothed and edges blur. A high-pass kernel has a large positive centre and negative neighbours: flat ground cancels to near zero and edges stand out.
A false colour composite shows near-infrared as red, red as green and green as blue, so healthy vegetation appears bright red and water dark.

A band ratio divides one band by another, pixel by pixel. Dividing cancels much of the illumination difference between a sunlit slope and a shaded one, so the ratio shows the material rather than the light falling on it.

blocks.where: ρ(NIR) and ρ(red) are reflectance or DN in the near-infrared and red bands; NDVI runs from −1 to +1; healthy crops approach 0.8, bare soil about 0.1 to 0.2, water and shadow are negative, and thick cloud stays close to zero.

blocks.text: Principal component analysis (PCA) rotates the bands into new uncorrelated axes called components, ordered by variance. The first component carries most of the brightness; later ones carry subtle spectral differences. Know what the method is for; the eigenvector working is rarely asked.

In supervised classification the analyst draws training areas for each class, using the visual keys of visual image interpretation. Software computes the mean and covariance of every class. The maximum likelihood rule then assigns each pixel to the class with the highest probability, assuming the class values follow a normal distribution.

In unsupervised classification there are no training areas. The k-means algorithm picks k clusters, seeds a mean for each, assigns every pixel to the nearest mean, recomputes the means, and repeats until the means stop moving. The analyst then names the clusters (water, crop, built-up) by looking at them on the image.

Supervised classification gives named classes directly but needs ground knowledge; unsupervised finds groups the analyst may not have expected and needs labelling afterwards. A majority filter then removes isolated single pixels.

Accuracy is judged against test pixels checked on the ground, listed in an error matrix (also called a confusion matrix) of mapped classes in rows against reference classes in columns. Overall accuracy is the diagonal sum divided by the total. User's accuracy of a class is its diagonal cell ÷ its row total: how often a pixel mapped as that class really is it. Producer's accuracy is the diagonal cell ÷ its column total: how much of the real class was found. Kappa removes the agreement that chance alone would produce.

blocks.where: p(o) is the observed agreement, the fraction of test pixels on the diagonal; p(e) is the agreement expected by chance from the row and column totals; κ = 1 is perfect agreement, κ = 0 is chance level.

examples.question: One band has digital numbers from 40 to 90. It is stretched linearly to the full 0–255 range. Write the stretch formula, find the output for input DN 40, 65 and 90, and state what happens to a pixel with DN 30.
steps: Ends from the histogram: min = 40, max = 90, so the range is 90 − 40 = 50. The stretch is DN(out) = (DN(in) − 40) ÷ 50 × 255 = 5.1 × (DN(in) − 40).
Input 65: 5.1 × 25 = 127.5; an 8-bit store holds whole numbers, so it is stored as 128.
Input 30: 5.1 × (−10) = −51, outside the display range, so it is clipped to 0.
examples.answer: The stretch gives DN 40 → 0, DN 65 → 127.5 (stored as 128) and DN 90 → 255; any DN below 40 clips to 0.

examples.question: A land-cover map is checked at 300 test pixels. Rows are the mapped class, columns the class found on the ground. Water row: 48, 2, 0. Crop row: 3, 120, 27. Built-up row: 1, 18, 81 (columns in the order water, crop, built-up). Find the overall accuracy, the user's and producer's accuracy of each class, and kappa.
steps: Row totals: water 48 + 2 + 0 = 50, crop 3 + 120 + 27 = 150, built-up 1 + 18 + 81 = 100. Column totals: water 48 + 3 + 1 = 52, crop 2 + 120 + 18 = 140, built-up 0 + 27 + 81 = 108. Grand total 300.
User's accuracy (diagonal ÷ row): water 48 ÷ 50 = 0.960, crop 120 ÷ 150 = 0.800, built-up 81 ÷ 100 = 0.810.
Producer's accuracy (diagonal ÷ column): water 48 ÷ 52 = 0.923, crop 120 ÷ 140 = 0.857, built-up 81 ÷ 108 = 0.750.
Reading: 27 real built-up pixels were mapped as crop, so built-up has the lowest producer's accuracy (0.750) even though 81 percent of what the map calls built-up is right.
examples.answer: Overall accuracy 0.830; user's accuracy 0.960, 0.800, 0.810 and producer's accuracy 0.923, 0.857, 0.750 for water, crop and built-up; κ = 0.725. The crop and built-up confusion is the weak point.

traps: High overall accuracy does not remove class confusion. A class can be right 95 percent of the time where the map shows it (user's accuracy) and still miss many of its real pixels (low producer's accuracy). Read both before trusting a class.
Radiometric correction is about brightness, geometric correction about position. Marks are lost by swapping the two.
A contrast stretch changes only the display values, not the stored reflectance. Do not claim it corrects the image.
NDVI is (NIR − red) ÷ (NIR + red). Reversing the order gives a negative index and a wrong map, and water genuinely has a negative NDVI.

User's accuracy divides by the row (mapped) total and producer's accuracy by the column (reference) total. Swapping them reverses the meaning: in the worked example built-up is 0.810 one way and 0.750 the other.

quiz.q: Define digital number and give the DN range of an 8-bit image.
quiz.a: The value stored in one pixel of one band; 0 to 255 for 8-bit.

quiz.q: Why does a raw image often look flat, and why does haze lift the darkest DN above zero?
quiz.a: The scene fills only a narrow part of the DN range, so contrast is low. Atmospheric scattering adds a near-constant path radiance to every pixel, so the minimum stays above zero.

quiz.q: A 3 × 3 low-pass kernel with all weights 1/9 covers a window of eight pixels with DN 10 and a centre pixel with DN 50. Find the output.
A crop gives NIR 0.40 and red 0.08 in sunlight and NIR 0.20 and red 0.04 on a shaded slope. Find the simple ratio NIR ÷ red in both places and say what it shows.
quiz.a: Sunlit: 0.40 ÷ 0.08 = 5.0. Shaded: 0.20 ÷ 0.04 = 5.0. Shade halves both bands, so the ratio is unchanged: it shows the material, not the light.

quiz.q: State two differences between supervised and unsupervised classification.
quiz.a: Supervised needs training areas chosen by the analyst and yields named classes directly. Unsupervised groups pixels by spectral similarity and needs the analyst to name the clusters afterwards.

quiz.q: A map reports 90 per cent overall accuracy but kappa 0.35. What does this tell you?
quiz.a: Much of the agreement could be chance, usually because one dominant class fills most of the map. Check the error matrix rows and columns for confused classes before trusting the map.

beyond: Not for the exam. Random forests, support vector machines and deep networks have largely replaced maximum likelihood in research, and object-based methods classify segments instead of single pixels. Cloud platforms let one analyst classify a whole state from a laptop, so accuracy assessment has become the formal part of the job. Search next for 'Sentinel-2 crop classification', 'random forest land cover' and 'confusion matrix kappa'.
